[[Survivable Airborne Operations Center]] (SAOC) }} The '''Boeing 747-8''', as ''-8i intercontinental'' for passengers and ''-8F freighter'', is the last member of the [[Boeing 747]] family, a series of [[Four-engined jet aircraft|four-engine]] long-range large [[Wide-body aircraft|wide-body airliners]] built by [[Boeing Commercial Airplanes]] until 2023. It is the largest model of the 747 that was introduced in the 1960s, and is Boeing's largest aircraft overall. Following the introduction of the [[747-400]]ER in 2000, Boeing explored larger 747 versions as potential competitors to the upcoming double-deck [[Airbus A380]] which had its maiden flight in 2005. The stretched 747, initially called the ''747 Advanced'', was officially launched as the 747-8 on November 14, 2005, with the designation reflecting its technological ties to the [[Boeing 787 Dreamliner|787 Dreamliner]] which first flew in 2009. At the time, Boeing forecast a market of 300 ''-8'' aircraft, but only about half as many were built. The 747-8's [[maiden flight]] was made by the freighter version, the 747-8F, on February 8, 2010, followed by the passenger version, the 747-8I Intercontinental, on March 20, 2011. The freighter version was delivered in October 2011, and the passenger variant entered commercial service in June 2012. The aircraft's [[fuselage]] was stretched by {{Convert|18|ft|abbr=out}}, reaching a total length of {{Convert|250|ft|abbr=out}}, making it the longest airliner in service. While retaining the basic structural design and wing sweep of its predecessors, the 747-8 has a deeper and thicker wing, allowing for greater fuel capacity, and larger [[raked wingtip]]s for improved aerodynamics. It is powered by a more efficient, smaller version of the [[General Electric GEnx]] turbofan engine from the 787 Dreamliner (recognizable by chevron edges on the engine nacelles). As a result, its [[maximum takeoff weight]] (MTOW) increases to {{Convert|975000|lb|t|abbr=out}}, making the 747-8 the heaviest Boeing airliner. The freighter version, with a shorter upper deck, can haul {{Convert|308000|lb|t|abbr=out}} over {{Convert|4120|nmi|abbr=~|lk=in}}. The intercontinental version can carry 467 passengers in a typical three-class configuration with a range of {{Convert|7790|nmi|abbr=out}}. A total of 155 aircraft were built including 107 freighters and 48 passenger airliners. The final aircraft, a 747-8F, was delivered to [[Atlas Air]] on January 31, 2023. == Development == === Background === {{main|Boeing 747}} [[File:Comparison of Boeing 747-400 and 747-500X.jpg|thumb|[[Boeing 747-400]] and 747-500X concept. The 747-500X fuselage would have been stretched by 18 ft (5.5 m) to 250 ft (76.2 m) long. The 747X and 747X Stretch derivatives were also proposed.]] [[Boeing]] had considered larger-capacity versions of the 747 several times during the 1990s (such as the [[Boeing New Large Airplane]]) and 2000s. The 747-500X and -600X, announced at the 1996 [[Farnborough Airshow]], would have stretched the 747,{{citation|title=Boeing Outlines the "Value" of its 747 Plans|url=http://www.boeing.com/news/releases/1996/news.release.960902c.html|website=Boeing website|date=September 2, 1996|access-date=April 5, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081024211719/http://www.boeing.com/news/releases/1996/news.release.960902c.html|archive-date=October 24, 2008|url-status=dead}} but they did not attract enough interest to enter development. At the same air show, a hypothetical wider-bodied 747-700X was described by a Boeing spokesperson as being possible, but inconsistent with the future requirements identified by the company. In 2000, Boeing offered the 747X and 747X Stretch derivatives as alternatives to the [[Airbus A380|Airbus A3XX]]. This was a more modest proposal than the previous −500X and −600X. The 747X would increase the 747's [[Wingspan#Wingspan of aircraft|wingspan]] to {{cvt|229|ft|sigfig=3}} by adding a segment at the root.[http://boeing.mediaroom.com/2000-01-21-Boeing-747-Celebrates-30-Years-In-Service "Boeing 747 Celebrates 30 Years In Service"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140529052510/http://boeing.mediaroom.com/2000-01-21-Boeing-747-Celebrates-30-Years-In-Service |date=May 29, 2014}}. Boeing, January 21, 2000. The 747X was to carry 430 passengers up to {{cvt|8700|nmi}}. The 747X Stretch would be extended to {{cvt|263|ft|sigfig=3}} long, allowing it to carry 500 passengers up to {{cvt|7800|nmi}}. However, the 747X family was unable to attract enough interest to enter production. Some of the ideas developed for the 747X were used on the [[Boeing 747-400#747-400ER|747-400ER]].[http://boeing.mediaroom.com/2000-11-28-Boeing-Launches-New-Longer-Range-747-400 "Boeing Launches New, Longer-Range 747-400"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140529052733/http://boeing.mediaroom.com/2000-11-28-Boeing-Launches-New-Longer-Range-747-400 |date=May 29, 2014}}. Boeing, November 28, 2000. After the 747X program, Boeing continued to study improvements to the 747. The 747-400XQLR (Quiet Long Range) was meant to have an increased range of {{cvt|8056|nmi}}, with better [[fuel efficiency]] and reduced [[Aircraft noise|noise]]. Changes studied included [[raked wingtips]] similar to those used on the 767-400ER and a '[[Chevron (aeronautics)|sawtooth]]' engine nacelle for noise reduction.[http://boeing.mediaroom.com/2002-02-26-Boeing-Offers-New-Quiet-Longer-Range-Version-of-747-400 "Boeing Offers New 747-400X Quiet Longer Range Jetliner"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140529052708/http://boeing.mediaroom.com/2002-02-26-Boeing-Offers-New-Quiet-Longer-Range-Version-of-747-400 |date=May 29, 2014}}. Boeing, February 26, 2002.[https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/boeing-favours-ge-for-latest-747-400-development-143990/ "Boeing favours GE for latest 747-400 development"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190216153104/https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/boeing-favours-ge-for-latest-747-400-development-143990/ |date=February 16, 2019}} Flight Global, March 5, 2002. Although the 747-400XQLR did not move to production, many of its features were used for the proposed ''747 Advanced.'' In early 2004, Boeing announced tentative plans for the 747 Advanced that were eventually adopted. Boeing selected the designation 747-8 for the aircraft to show the technology connection between the [[Boeing 787 Dreamliner]] and the new 747.{{Cite web |last=Kingsley-Jones |first=Max |date=November 13, 2012 |title=IN FOCUS: Boeing 747-8 technical description & cutaway |url=https://www.flightglobal.com/in-focus-boeing-747-8-technical-description-and-cutaway/107801.article |access-date=January 10, 2025 |website=Flight Global |language=en}}{{Cite web |title=747-8 Over Mt. Rainier |url=https://secure.boeingimages.com/archive/747-8-Over-Mt--Rainier-2F3XC5KLE2I.html |access-date=January 10, 2024 |website=Boeing |quote=By working together with customers and applying the innovative new technologies of the 787 Dreamliner, Boeing was able to create the 747-8 family. In fact, the designation 747-8 was chosen to show the technology connection between the 787 and the new 747.}} The 747-8 used technology and the [[General Electric GEnx]] engines from the 787 to modernize the design and its systems.[http://boeing.mediaroom.com/2004-02-09-Boeing-747-the-Queen-of-the-Skies-Celebrates-35th-Anniversary "Boeing 747, the 'Queen of the Skies,' Celebrates 35th Anniversary"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171009034309/http://boeing.mediaroom.com/2004-02-09-Boeing-747-the-Queen-of-the-Skies-Celebrates-35th-Anniversary |date=October 9, 2017}}. Boeing, February 9, 2004. In 2005, Boeing forecast a market for 300 aircraft, split evenly between freighters and passenger variants.{{cite magazine |url= http://archive.aviationweek.com/issue/20051031 |author= Robert Wall |title= Counterclaims |quote= Boeing talks up 747 Advanced, talks down Airbus A350 |magazine= Aviation Week & Space Technology |date= October 31, 2005 |page= 40 |url-access= subscription |access-date= November 13, 2018 |archive-date= November 13, 2018 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20181113165850/http://archive.aviationweek.com/issue/20051031 |url-status= live}} ===Design effort=== [[File:Boeing Everett Plant.jpg|thumb|Boeing's [[Boeing Everett Factory|Everett Facility]] at [[Paine Field]], originally built for the 747 program, is the site of 747-8 assembly.]] On November 14, 2005, Boeing announced the launching of the 747 Advanced as the "Boeing 747-8".{{cite web |url= http://boeing.mediaroom.com/2005-11-14-Boeing-Launches-New-747-8-Family |title= Boeing Launches New 747-8 Family |publisher= Boeing |date= November 14, 2005 |access-date= December 17, 2007 |archive-date= September 21, 2013 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20130921054840/http://boeing.mediaroom.com/2005-11-14-Boeing-Launches-New-747-8-Family |url-status= live}} The 747-8 was the first lengthened 747 to go into production and the second 747 version with a fuselage of modified length after the shortened [[Boeing 747SP|747SP]]. The 747-8 was intended to use the same engine and [[cockpit]] technology as that of the 787, including the [[General Electric GEnx]] [[turbofan]] and [[fly-by-wire]] ailerons and spoilers.[http://www.aviationweek.com/aw/generic/story_channel.jsp?channel=comm&id=news/OUT04118.xml "Boeing Rethinks 747-8 Outsourcing"]. ''Aviation Week'', April 11, 2008. {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111106074210/http://www.aviationweek.com/aw/generic/story_channel.jsp?channel=comm&id=news%2FOUT04118.xml |date=November 6, 2011}} In 2006, Boeing said that the new design would be quieter, more economical and more [[environmentally friendly]] than previous versions of the 747. As a derivative of the already-common [[Boeing 747-400|747-400]], the 747-8 has the economic benefit of similar training and [[interchangeable parts]]. Boeing firmed the 747-8 Freighter's configuration in October 2006.[https://web.archive.org/web/20061110052246/http://www.boeing.com/news/releases/2006/q4/061030g_nr.html "Boeing Completes Firm Configuration of 747-8 Freighter"]. Boeing The {{not a typo|747-8}}, as a new development of Boeing's largest airliner, is notably in direct competition on long-haul routes with the [[Airbus A380]], a full-length [[double-deck aircraft]] introduced in 2007. For airlines seeking very large passenger airliners, the two have been pitched as [[Competition between Airbus and Boeing|competitors]] on various occasions. Boeing states that the 747-8 is more than 10 percent lighter per seat and consumes 11 percent less fuel per passenger than the A380, translating into a trip-cost reduction of 21 percent and a seat-mile cost reduction of over 6 percent.{{cite web |title=Boeing 747-8 Intercontinental and 747-8 Freighter |publisher=Boeing |url=http://www.boeing.com/boeing/commercial/747family/747-8_facts.page |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141021171911/http://www.boeing.com/boeing/commercial/747family/747-8_facts.page |archive-date=October 21, 2014 |access-date=July 1, 2011}} Production of the first 747-8 Freighter began in Everett in early August 2008.Dunlop, Michelle. Boeing, July 21, 2009. In October 2009, Boeing announced that it had delayed the first flight on the 747-8 until the first quarter of 2010 and delayed 747-8I delivery. ''Aviation Today'', March 26, 2009. ==Variants== ===747-8 Freighter=== [[File:UPS Boeing 747-8F N611UP.jpg|alt=A white, black and yellow four-engined wide-body cargo jetliner about to land|thumb|A Boeing 747-8 Freighter of [[UPS Airlines]], its largest operator.]] The 747-400 and earlier versions had proven to be a very popular [[Freight aircraft|freighter]], carrying around half of the world's air freight."[https://web.archive.org/web/20121011082258/http://www.boeing.com/commercial/747family/freighter/ Boeing 747-400 Freighter Family: The World's Best Freighters]." [[File:Interior Boeing 747-8 Intercontinental main deck.jpg|thumb|Main deck [[Business Class]] seating on the 747-8 Intercontinental]] During the initial 747-8 marketing phase, Boeing also proposed creating a revenue-generating "SkyLoft" passenger facility in the crown space above the [[cabin (aircraft)|cabin]]. This facility would include "SkySuites", small individual compartments with sliding doors or curtains, featuring beds, seating, and entertainment or business equipment. A common [[wikt:Lounge|lounge]] area could also be provided. Boeing also proposed smaller, more modest "SkyBunks". Access to the crown area would be via a separate stairway at the rear of the aircraft. Passengers using the SkySuites, sold at a premium price, would sit in regular [[economy class]] seats for take-off and landing, and move to the crown area during flight. However, pricing feasibility studies found the SkyLoft concept difficult to justify. ==Incidents== {{Further|topic=GEnx Engine Issues|GEnx#Operational history}} On September 11, 2012, an [[AirBridgeCargo Airlines|AirBridgeCargo]] 747-8F experienced a major engine malfunction that spread a significant amount of metallic debris on the runway. Like in a similar event with the [[GEnx|GEnx Engine]] during pre-flight taxi tests on a [[Boeing 787 Dreamliner|Boeing 787]], the low-pressure turbine shaft separated and shifted backwards, damaging the low-pressure turbine blades and vanes.{{cite web |url=http://avherald.com/h?article=455c2b52&opt=0 |author=Simon Hradecky |title=Incident: Air Bridge Cargo B748 at Shanghai on Sep 11th 2012, rejected takeoff}} The NTSB issued urgent safety recommendations to the FAA to require ultrasonic scans for midshaft fractures before use of GEnx engines and require repetitive on-wing inspections of the engine to detect cracks.{{Cite web |url=https://www.ntsb.gov/news/press-releases/Pages/NTSB_issues_urgent_recommendations_for_GEnx-1B_and_-2B_engines.aspx |title=NTSB issues urgent recommendations for GEnx-1B and -2B engines |access-date=December 27, 2019 |archive-date=December 27, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191227102454/https://www.ntsb.gov/news/press-releases/Pages/NTSB_issues_urgent_recommendations_for_GEnx-1B_and_-2B_engines.aspx |url-status=live}} On July 31, 2013, an AirBridgeCargo 747-8F experienced core engine icing that caused engine malfunctions and damage to three engines near [[Chengdu, China]], while en route to [[Hong Kong]]; the aircraft landed safely at its destination.
